newsitem.title: UK: Full text of April 10 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of April 10 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: Following is the full text of the mniutes of the April 10 monetary meeting between former Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England met, together with officials, on 10 April, to review monetary developments.
Monetary and Economic Developments

2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by officials before the meeting) confirmed that cost pressures remained moderate, although the labour market continued to tighten. There were continuing signs that activity remained strong, with growth strongest in services and demand concentrated on the consumer side.
Inflation Indicators

3.Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest payments - RPIX) fell as expected by 0.2 percentage points in February, to 2.9 per cent, due to falls in the inflation rates for food and consumer durables. All-items RPI inflation fell by 0.1 percentage point, to 2.7 per cent.
4.Most other indicators confirmed that non-labour cost pressures remained moderate, although earnings growth picked up again:
-- sterling non-oil commodity prices rose by 0.2 per cent in February, but were 4.5 per cent lower than a year ago. The oil price had fallen again sharply, to $17.0 per barrel;
-- after initially falling back, sterling's effective exchange rate index had risen further from 98.1 before the last meeting, to 99.3 currently;

-- total non-oil import prices fell by 3.8 per cent in the three months to January compared to the previous three months, and were 5.3 per cent lower than a year earlier. Non-EU import prices fell by 2.2 per cent in the three months to February on the previous three months;

-- producer input prices for manufacturing (excluding food, beverage, tobacco and petroleum industries) were unchanged in February; but compared to a year earlier they were 7.4 per cent lower. The CIPS manufacturing survey indicated further falls in non-wage input prices in March; but the new CIPS survey for services indicated rising input costs in March, mainly reflecting wage costs;

-- producer output prices (excluding FBTP) rose by 0.1 per cent in February; but the annual inflation rate fell to 0.5 per cent, from 0.6 per cent in January. The CBI survey output price expectations balance rose in March, but remained well below its long-run average;
-- the annual growth rate of underlying average earnings rose sharply in January, to 5.0 per cent; but IRS median pay settlements were unchanged at 3.0 per cent in January.
Monetary and Financial Indicators

5. Notes and coin grew by 0.5 per cent in March, following a 0.2 per cent rise in February; and the annual growth rate rose slightly, to 6.4 per cent. M0's annual growth rate was unchanged, at 6.4 per cent.
6. M4 grew by 1.4 per cent in February, after rising by 1.7 per cent in January. The annual growth rate of M4 and M4 lending rose, to 11.3 per cent, and 9.3 per cent, respectively.

7.The Halifax house price index rose by 1.0 per cent in March, giving an annual increase of 7.2 per cent. The Nationwide index rose by 1.6 per cent in March, and was 9.7 per cent up on a year earlier. Housing market transactions continued to rise; in the three months to February particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) were 5.3 per cent up on the previous three months, and 28.0 per cent higher than a year earlier.

8. Short-term interest rates were little changed in Germany and Japan since the last meeting, but had risen by around 25 basis points in the US following the quarter point rise in official rates. UK short-term interest rates had risen by over 20 basis points; and forward rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts had risen at all maturities (by less than 20 basis points for June but nearly 40 basis points for December and March).

9. 10-year bond yields had risen by over 30 basis points in the US and by over 40 basis points in Germany, but had fallen by over 20 basis points in Japan. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts had risen at all maturities (by up to 40 basis points). Since the last meeting inflation expectations implied by the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) had risen by nearly 20 basis points for 5 years ahead, and 25 basis points for 10 years ahead.
Activity Indicators

10. In the US recent data suggested that output was growing above trend. The latest estimate of GDP growth in Q4 was 0.9 per cent (not annualised), following growth of 0.5 per cent in Q3. Industrial production rose by 0.5 per cent in February, following a fall of 0.1 per cent in January. In Japan industrial production fell by 3.4 per cent (not annualised) in February, following a rise of 5.6 per cent in January.

11. In Germany the latest estimate of GDP growth in Q4 was 0.1 per cent, leaving it 1.4 per cent up on a year earlier. Industrial production rose by 1.9 per cent in February, following a fall of 1.5 per cent in January. Unemployment fell back slightly in March, to 11.2 per cent. In France the latest estimate of GDP growth in Q4 was 0.2 per cent, leaving it 1.2 per cent up on a year earlier.

12. The latest estimate of UK GDP growth in Q4 showed that whole economy and non-oil GDP both grew by 0.8 per cent, and were respectively 2.6 per cent and 2.5 per cent up on a year earlier. Consumer spending rose by 0.9 per cent in Q4, leaving it 4.0 per cent higher than a year earlier. Investment rose by 2.3 per cent in Q4, and was 2.3 per cent up on a year earlier.
13. Most other activity data were consistent with output growth continuing at or above trend, and indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were more buoyant:

-- manufacturing output rose by 0.2 per cent in February, and in the three months to February it was up 1.6 per cent on a year earlier. Total industrial output fell by 0.6 per cent in February reflecting a fall in energy output, but in the latest three months was up 1.9 per cent on a year earlier;

-- major business surveys continued to point to continuing growth in activity. The March CIPS and CBI surveys both showed a rise in orders for manufacturing, and the indicators of output growth remained above their long-run averages. The new CIPS survey on services showed strong and increasing growth in the service sector;
-- retail sales volumes rose by 0.5 per cent in February; and in the latest three months they were 4.0 per cent higher than a year earlier;

-- and latest survey indicators in the retail sector indicated continuing sales growth: consumer confidence fell slightly in March, but remained on a firm upward trend; the March CBI Distributive Trades Survey showed a slight rise in the balance of retailers expecting higher sales; and the February BRC survey showed continuing sales growth;

-- claimant unemployment fell by 68,200 in February, to its lowest level since October 1990, and the unemployment rate fell to 6.2 per cent; but the figures were still distorted by the introduction of the Job Seekers Allowance. Unfilled vacancies at Jobcentres rose by 7,800 in February, to their highest level since the series began in January 1980.
Summary of discussion

14. The Governor said that since the meeting on 5 March the exchange rate - particularly against the Continental European currencies and the Yen - had strengthened somewhat further, and this continued to act as a brake on inflation in the short term. At the same time the monetary data, and the data on domestic demand and on output, had been uniformly strong, and that reinforced the Bank's concern that the inflation target was now at significant risk looking two years ahead.

15. The exchange rate, in effective terms, had risen to a 4-year high of 99.4 compared with 98.1 at the time of the last meeting. It had now risen by 19 per cent over the past year - by 6 per cent against the $, by 23 per cent against the DM and by 25 per cent against the Yen.

16. The Governor said there was no doubt that sterling's appreciation was having a dampening effect on costs and prices in the short term, but perhaps less of an effect, so far at least, than might have been expected.

17. Non-oil import prices had fallen by 0.2 per cent in January, and by 4.2 per cent in the six months to January despite the 12 per cent rise in the sterling effective exchange rate over the same period. And according to provisional estimates, the price of goods imported from non-EU countries (excluding oil) had risen by 1.1 per cent in February.

18. The Governor noted that cost pressures early in the supply chain remained weak. The Bank's sterling commodity price index had fallen by 2.5 per cent in February and was 2.7 per cent lower than a year earlier. That was mainly due to sharp falls in the price of crude oil: the monthly average of the sterling one-month future price of Brent crude was 10.2 per cent lower in February than in January, and had fallen sharply further in March. Excluding oil, sterling commodity prices had in fact risen, by 1.8 per cent, over the past 3 months, despite the exchange rate appreciation.

19. Manufacturers' costs remained subdued. Input prices had fallen again in February, by 0.5 per cent, despite unexpected rises in the prices of most imported input goods. That had left the index 6.6 per cent below the level a year earlier.

20. Manufacturers continued to pass on much of the benefit of these lower cost pressures. The twelve-month increase in manufacturing output prices (excluding excise duties) had fallen again, from 1.0 per cent in January to 0.6 per cent in February. And output prices (excluding FBTP) had risen by only 0.5 per cent in the twelve months to February, the lowest annual rise for nearly thirty years.

21.The Governor said that at the retail level, annual RPIX inflation had fallen from 3.1 per cent in January to 2.9 per cent in February - a somewhat smaller fall than the Bank had expected. The general pattern of rising service sector inflation and falling goods price inflation had continued. There was some evidence of the effect of sterling's appreciation in the food and consumer durables sectors; but elsewhere - in clothing and footwear - inflation had risen unexpectedly. It was difficult yet to say whether that reflected a smaller, or simply a delayed, pass-through of sterling's appreciation than had been originally anticipated. The expectation that service sector and goods price inflation would continue to diverge this year seemed intact, given the relative strength of service sector demand and cost pressures.

22. Perhaps partly because of the relatively limited price effects of the appreciation so far there had also been less impact on recorded trade volumes than might have been feared. Net exports of goods and services had made a positive contribution of 0.2 percentage points to GDP growth in Q4, unchanged from the preliminary estimate. That reflected growth in exports of 2.3 per cent and growth in imports of 1.6 per cent. Service exports had risen strongly in the quarter, up by 4.6 per cent. Goods exports had risen by 1.7 per cent in Q4 to be 6.7 per cent higher than a year earlier. There continued nevertheless to be a good deal of anecdotal and survey evidence of weakening export orders.

23. Notwithstanding these relatively limited effects so far, the Bank continued to assume that the appreciation would reduce the rate of retail price inflation to below 2 per cent in the course of this year; and that it would lead to a weakening of net external demand.
24. On the other hand, the Governor said, there was now compelling evidence of the strength of the domestic economy.

25. Real GDP had risen by 0.8 per cent in the final quarter of 1996 - an annualised rate of 3 per cent in H2 - unchanged from February's estimate. But, in terms of the expenditure components, there had been upward revisions to fixed investment and public consumption, and downward revisions to stockbuilding. Growth in final domestic demand, therefore, had been revised up from a preliminary estimate of 0.6 per cent to 1.2 per cent in Q4 - its highest growth rate since the beginning of 1989. And the difference between the various measures of GDP remained: in Q4, the level of the expenditure measure of GDP was still 0.7 percentage points below the average measure of GDP, suggesting the possibility of upward revision.

26. Consumption expenditure had risen by 0.9 per cent in Q4, or at an annualised rate of 3-1/2 per cent in H2, well above its long-run average growth rate. Much of the growth was based in expenditure on services, particularly transport and communication and financial services. The Bank expected growth in consumption expenditure to remain strong in the first quarter of 1997. The volume of retail sales had risen by 0.7 per cent in January and a further 0.5 per cent in February. Even if sales were unchanged in March, growth in Q1 would be just below 1 per cent.

27. In the housing market, annual house price inflation had remained strong in March: 7.2 per cent according to the Halifax index and 9.7 per cent according to the Nationwide index. After rising rapidly over the past year housing market activity may have levelled off. In the three months to February private housing starts had fallen by 1 per cent, though they remained 24 per cent up on a year earlier.

28. Fixed investment was estimated to have increased by 2.3 per cent in Q4, up from the initial estimate of 0.2 per cent - although it had been revised down for 1996 as a whole. Private investment had risen by 6.4 per cent in Q4, though business investment rose by only 0.7 per cent, which was surprising: profitability remained high with ICCs' trading profits up by nearly 16 per cent over the year to Q4. Investment in housing had risen by 2.5 per cent on the quarter - and by an average annual rate of 11 per cent since Q1 1996.
29. The Governor noted that the latest monthly output

data, for February, showed that, although industrial production weakened (by 0.6 per cent) because of the effect of the warmer weather on energy production, manufacturing output had increased by 0.2 per cent on the month - unusually for the third month in succession - and at an annual rate of 2.5 per cent over the last three months. The new CIPS survey of services showed that activity in that sector had accelerated in both February and March.

30. The labour market had continued to tighten by more than expected. Unemployment had fallen by a further 68,200 in February bringing the unemployment rate down by 0.3 percentage points to 6.2 per cent, though this probably exaggerated the underlying fall because of the effect of the Job Seekers Allowance.
31. The Workforce in Employment had risen by 0.2 per cent

(47,000) in Q4 following a revised increase of 0.8 per cent (216,000) in Q3. The annual rate of increase was 0.9 per cent in the year to Q4. The rise in Q4 was more than accounted for by a rise in full-time employment, perhaps suggesting a stronger rise in total hours than indicated by the headline employment figures alone. Much of the growth in recent quarters had been outside the manufacturing sector, which remained consistent with the general picture on activity; manufacturing employment had risen by 0.4 per cent (15,000) in January but was only 0.3 per cent up on the same period a year ago. Vacancies had risen by 7,800 in February to 270,900, the highest stock ever recorded; and the Bank's agents were reporting more evidence of skill shortages.

32. Whole economy underlying average earnings growth had been revised up by per cent in December to 4-3/4 per cent, and had risen further to 5 per cent in January (compared with only 3-1/2 per cent in the year to January 1996). The increase had been more marked in services, but underlying growth in both services and production sectors now stood at 5 per cent (4-3/4 per cent in manufacturing). Even allowing for the effect of bonuses in recent months, particularly in the financial services sector, earnings growth was now close to the limit of what could be sustained consistently with the inflation target in the medium term.

33. There was, however, as yet little upward pressure on wage settlements, with the 3-month employment weighted average falling slightly in February, to 3.1 per cent from a revised 3.2 per cent in January. It had been broadly stable at around this level over the past year.

34. The Governor said that broad money growth had remained strong in February. The twelve-month growth rate of M4, now broadly free of gilt repo distortions, was over 11 per cent in February, its highest since 1990. The twelve-month growth rate of M4 lending was 9.3 per cent. Underlying money and credit growth had been in a range of 8-10 per cent for at least 18 months, with M4 generally in the upper half, and credit the lower half of this range. February's data took M4 above this range, and lending into the upper half. Some of the effects of persistent strength in money growth had already begun to show up in nominal GDP growth. This had been led by higher consumption - consistent with the earlier pick-up in personal sector M4. On past relationships, the Bank would expect the strength of companies' M4 to be reflected in higher investment too during 1997.

35. Narrow money growth, which had slowed in February, picked up in March. Notes and coin grew by 0.5 per cent on the month (compared with 0.2 per cent in February) and by 6.4 per cent on a year earlier - still somewhat below the 7 to 7-1/2 per cent annual rate of growth seen in H2 last year.

36. The Governor said that the last few months' data had confirmed the overall picture which the Bank had expected towards the end of last year, when it started to press for a tightening of monetary policy. It had perhaps been possible to argue that weakness of some of the December numbers - for example manufacturing production, retail sales and broad money - provided justification for postponing a move. But it was now clear that those numbers had been essentially erratic.

37. It was true that in the short term inflationary pressures had weakened - though perhaps by less than might have been expected - helped by sterling's appreciation. And those pressures were likely to remain subdued in the period ahead. But overall demand continued to grow clearly above trend and the monetary data in particular suggested that the risks were more on the upside. The need for a tightening of monetary policy, if we were to stand any reasonable chance of meeting the inflation target two years ahead, had therefore become more urgent; and the Bank continued to recommend making a start now by raising interest rates by a 1/4 per cent.

38. The Chancellor said he was not persuaded of the case for increasing interest rates in April. The pound had strengthened further since the last meeting. If anything, the policy dilemma had got worse. The question was not only what effect would the stronger pound inevitably have on activity, but also where the pound would go if a small rise in interest rates was taken to be a signal of further increases to come.

39. The Chancellor said that he could see two possible explanations for the movements in sterling. Firstly, it was the counterpart of weakness in the Deutschmark, which was due to EMU uncertainties - either that EMU would be delayed, or that it would proceed on time but the euro would be weak. Secondly, the markets were anticipating interest rate increases in the UK. They were aware that the Bank had advised that interest rates should rise. Also, market expectations were building that, whatever the outcome of the election, there would follow a period of increases in interest rates.

40. The pound was now back within its old ERM bands and it was still rising. It was nearing a level where businesses would begin to feel the effects on their competitiveness. The pound had risen by 1-1/2 per cent since the last meeting. Compared to a year ago it was nearly 25 per cent up on both the Deutschmark and the yen, and 19 per cent up on the trade weighted index.

41. The Chancellor said that he did not have an exchange rate target. But an exchange rate movement of this magnitude would have a similar effect on activity and inflation to a rise in interest rates. It was clear that the effects would not be negligible, even though the effects on activity from the stronger pound had been slow to come through so far.

42. The Chancellor said that he and the Governor were only a 1/4 percentage point apart on interest rates. But he was concerned that even a small rise in interest rates might be viewed by the markets as the first in a series of interest rate increases. This could cause the pound to rise further.

43. Activity was strong, and growing a little above trend. Before Christmas some had expected growth to accelerate rapidly, but this had not happened. GDP was up 2.6 per cent on a year earlier in the fourth quarter. Within that total, manufacturing remained subdued, up 0.2 per cent in February and up 1.6 per cent on a year earlier.

44. The Chancellor said that consumer demand was strong, with retail sales up 4 per cent in the three months to February on a year earlier. House prices were rising at between 7 and 10 per cent a year. But in his view, prices were plainly being driven up by a shortage of supply. As more property came on to the market, he did not think these rates of house price inflation would be sustained. There were signs that market activity had calmed down already particulars delivered fell back in February. The housing market was recovering, but in a steady and sustainable manner.

45. Producer price inflation was very subdued, especially input price inflation which was benefitting from falls in oil prices. The labour market was recovering strongly and there were some early signs of a tightening evident from anecdotal reports of skill shortages and poaching of staff by companies. Also, vacancies were high. However, given the effects of the Job Seekers Allowance it was difficult to estimate the trend in unemployment.

46. Earnings growth had picked up, but some of the rise was due to bonus payments. Settlements had not moved for a considerable period of time and remained at around 3 per cent. Growth in broad money had moved into a higher gear, and was beginning to become a significant concern. However, it was somewhat puzzling that narrow money growth had remained so stable.

47. But the Chancellor's overwhelming view was that nothing had moved on much since Christmas, except for growing market expectations about an imminent rise in interest rates as early as May. The underlying arguments had not changed in recent months. And it was premature to take a view on any change in rates at subsequent meetings - that would depend on the data. But he remained concerned that an increase in interest rates could cause further rises in the pound.

48. In the Chancellor's view the recovery was continuing, and there were no indications yet of big inflationary pressures two years out. He thought that the inflation target would still be hit if interest rates stayed where they were for the moment.
49. In discussion the following points were made:

-- most of the indicators of demand, activity and the labour market had strengthened in recent months, pointing to some rise in inflation pressures in the future. The main countervailing factor was the exchange rate, although the strength of domestic demand was allowing firms to put up prices and pay despite the exchange rate;

-- there were some signs that the rising exchange rate was having an effect on export orders and manufacturing activity. However, the prospects were that the strength of domestic demand would continue to outweigh the effect of the exchange rate on activity;

-- the exchange rate had also led to lower input prices for firms, and some limited effect on retail prices. On the harmonised indices of consumer prices, inflation in the UK was around the EU average even though the UK's economic recovery was further advanced. But in order to be consistent with the inflation target, the higher exchange rate would be expected to have temporarily taken inflation below 2-1/2 per cent;

-- the high exchange rate had led to some tightening of monetary conditions. Without that influence, interest rates would have had to rise sooner. However, to the extent that the exchange rate was supported by the expectation that interest rates would rise, if rates were not raised the pound might fall back again. Also the effect of the stronger exchange rate was concentrated on the trade sector, where many firms already had spare capacity. Much of the rise in inflation pressures (on both pay and prices) was concentrated in the service sector, which would be affected less by the exchange rate;

-- it was not clear how the exchange rate might react to a rise in interest rates. Markets were currently expecting interest rates to rise in the near future. If rates were raised against that background, the impact on the exchange rate might be limited. However, if markets interpreted an interest rate rise as increasing the likelihood of more substantial rises to follow, that could put further upward pressure on the exchange rate.
Conclusion

50. In summary, the Chancellor said that there remained a small difference of judgement between himself and the Governor. There were signs that activity had strengthened somewhat recently; but he expected the stronger exchange rate to have a further impact on growth, and hence inflation. He was not persuaded that the current level of interest rates was inconsistent with achieving the inflation target, and he decided to leave them unchanged for the moment.
H M Treasury
